claim: Five cryoEM structures of human ORC were determined: ORCO2-5 (3.5 Å), ORCO1AAA (3.2 Å), ORCO2WH (3.7 Å), ORCOPEN (4.0 Å), and ORCDNA (4.3 Å).
source: The cryoEM analysis lead to a 3.5 Å structure of the ORC2-5 complex (ORCO2-5) and four distinct structures of the ORC1-5 complex: ORCO1AAA (3.2 Å), ORCO2WH (3.7 Å), ORCOPEN (4.0 Å), and ORCDNA (4.3 Å) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–4 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolutions of all five structures determined in this study.

claim: The ORCO2-5 structure lacks the ORC1 subunit and consists of subunits ORC2-5 in a compact and substantially closed conformation.
source: The ORCO2-5 structure that lacks the ORC1 subunit consists of subunits ORC2-5 in a compact and substantially closed conformation (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structure and Figure 1b shows the ORCO2-5 structure.

claim: In ORCO2-5, the ORC2 WHD is collapsed into the ring-shaped core of the complex with the β-hairpin wing facing the ORC4 WHD.
source: The ORC2 WHD of ORCO2-5 is collapsed into the ring-shaped core of the complex with the β-hairpin wing facing the ORC4 WHD (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript describes the position of ORC2 WHD in ORCO2-5 and references Figure 2c.

claim: The ORC2 WHD in ORCO2-5 is rotated ~135° compared to the auto-inhibited state of ORC2 WHD in the DmORC structure.
source: The ORC2 WHD is significantly deeper in the core and rotated ~135° compared to the auto-inhibited state of ORC2 WHD in the DmORC structure (Figure 2d and Video 1; Bleichert et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific rotation angle and cites the DmORC structure for comparison.

claim: In ORCO2WH, the ORC1 AAA+ domain is dynamic and unresolved in the refined map.
source: The first of these, ORCO2WH, consists of a dynamic ORC1 AAA+ domain that is unresolved in the refined map (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the ORC1 AAA+ domain is unresolved in ORCO2WH.

claim: In ORCO2WH, the ORC2 WHD is stably bound inside the ring-shaped core in a conformation similar to the auto-inhibited state observed in DmORC.
source: Interestingly, in this structure, the ORC2 WHD was stably bound inside the ring-shaped core of ORC in a conformation that is similar to the auto-inhibited state observed in the DmORC structure (Figure 2d,f; Bleichert et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ORC2 WHD conformation in ORCO2WH and compares it to DmORC.

claim: In ORCO1AAA, the ORC2 WHD is dynamic and unresolved in the refined map.
source: In contrast to ORCO2WH, ORCO1AAA consists of a dynamic ORC2 WHD that is unresolved in the refined map (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the ORC2 WHD is unresolved in ORCO1AAA.

claim: In ORCO1AAA, the ORC1 AAA+ domain is ordered and forms an interface with ORC4 with an ATP coordinated between the two subunits.
source: The ORC1 AAA+ domain in this structure is ordered and forms the important interface with ORC4 with an ATP coordinated between the two subunits, an ATPase active conformation seen in previous ScORC and HsORC structures (Li et al., 2018; Tocilj et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ORC1 AAA+ domain in ORCO1AAA and cites previous structures.

claim: Three ATP nucleotides were well resolved in the ORC maps.
source: Three ATP nucleotides were well resolved in the ORC maps (Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous observations (Tocilj et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript states that three ATP molecules were resolved and references figures showing them.

claim: Magnesium ions were resolved in the ORC maps and were likely retained from the protein expression lysate.
source: Although not provided in the sample buffer, magnesium ions were also resolved in the maps and were likely retained from the protein expression lysate.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that magnesium ions were observed despite not being added to the buffer.

claim: In ORCO2WH, an ATP is absent at the ORC1·4 site due to the displacement of the ORC1 AAA+-domain.
source: Only in the ORCO2WH structure was an ATP absent at the ORC1·4 site due to the displacement of the ORC1 AAA+-domain (Figure 1c, Figure 2a,b and Video 2) and consequential disruption of the ATP binding site.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that ATP is absent at the ORC1·4 site in ORCO2WH.

claim: The ORC1·4 site is the only site that has been shown to have ATPase activity.
source: Of the three ATP-binding sites, only the ORC1·4 site exhibits ATPase activity and this activity is essential for cell viability (Bowers et al., 2004; Klemm et al., 1997; Randell et al., 2006; Tocilj et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript states that only the ORC1·4 site exhibits ATPase activity and cites multiple studies.

claim: Mutations at the ORC1·4 ATPase site are associated with Meier-Gorlin Syndrome.
source: In addition, several mutations at the ORC1·4 ATPase site are associated with the developmental disorder Meier-Gorlin Syndrome (Bicknell et al., 2011a; Bicknell et al., 2011b; de Munnik et al., 2012a; de Munnik et al., 2012b; Guernsey et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the association between ORC1·4 mutations and Meier-Gorlin Syndrome with multiple citations.

claim: The ORC5·3 interface appears considerably more flexible relative to the other ATP interfaces.
source: The ORC1·4 and ORC4·5 sites represent canonical AAA+ ATPase sites (Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2008; Erzberger and Berger, 2006), while the ORC5·3 interface is considerably more flexible relative to the other ATP interfaces.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the ORC5·3 interface as more flexible.

claim: ORC3 does not seem to participate in ATP coordination at the ORC5·3 interface.
source: In contrast to ORC1·4 and ORC4·5, the ORC5·3 interface appears considerably more flexible and, in fact, ORC3 does not seem to participate in ATP coordination (Figure 1g).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that ORC3 does not participate in ATP coordination.

claim: The solvent-accessible surface area buried between ORC2 and ORC3 (3296 Å2) is significantly larger than between ORC4 and ORC5 (2707 Å2).
source: The solvent-accessible surface area buried between ORC2 and ORC3 (3296 Å2) is significantly larger than the next closest interacting subunits ORC4 and ORC5 (2707 Å2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific surface area measurements for subunit interfaces.

claim: ORC2 and ORC3 localize to centromeres in mitosis and may function independently of the other ORC subunits.
source: In fact, ORC2 and ORC3 localize to centromeres in mitosis and may function independently of the other ORC subunits (Craig et al., 2003; Prasanth et al., 2004; Prasanth et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing ORC2 and ORC3 localization to centromeres.

claim: In ORCOPEN, the ORC2·3 subunits rotate away from the ORC1·4·5 motor module by 22° at a hinge originating from the ORC3·5 interface.
source: When aligned to ORCO1AAA, a hinge in ORCOPEN is evident and originates from the somewhat loose ORC3·5 interface, allowing the ORC2·3 subunits (including the ORC5 WH) to rotate (22° rotation angle) away from the ORC1·4·5 motor module in a hinge motion (Figure 3a).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific rotation angle and describes the hinge motion.

claim: The ORC3 N-terminal region in ORCOPEN consists of an extended, straightened α-helix (aa42-86) that is bent in other ORC conformations by 32°.
source: In addition, the ORC3 N-terminal region of ORCOPEN consists of an extended, straightened α-helix (aa42-86) that is bent in the other ORC conformations by 32° (Figure 1e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific residue numbers and a bending angle.

claim: Multibody refinement revealed two prominent movements of ORC: twisting and pinching, both emanating from the hinge at the ORC3·5 interface.
source: The two movements can be described as twisting and pinching, respectively, both emanating from the hinge at the ORC3·5 interface (Figure 3c,d and Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the two types of movements observed in multibody refinement.

claim: The twisting and pinching movements contributed between 17% to 23% of the total variance of each particle population.
source: These movements contributed between 17% to 23% of the total variance of each particle population.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for the contribution of these movements.

claim: DNA was detected in the affinity-purified, recombinant HsORC expressed in Sf9 insect cells.
source: DNA was detected in the affinity-purified, recombinant HsORC expressed in Sf9 insect cells and the presence of this DNA species was only detected when ORC was expressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The manuscript states that DNA was detected in the purified ORC sample.

claim: In ORCDNA, DNA contacts are made by all five subunits of ORC, with the most significant interactions occurring with the ORC1 RecA-fold and ORC2 WHD.
source: The structure shows DNA contacts by all five subunits of ORC, with the most significant interactions occurring with the ORC1 RecA-fold and ORC2 WHD (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: The manuscript describes DNA contacts with all five ORC subunits.

claim: In the ORC1 RecA-fold, two loops (residues 593–596 and 626–630) are in close contact with DNA.
source: In the ORC1 RecA-fold, two loops (residues 593–596 and 626–630, respectively) at the N-terminal regions of two α-helices are in close contact to the DNA.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific residue numbers for loops contacting DNA.

claim: Several positively-charged and aromatic residues in ORC1 loops (K591, N595, H596 W626, H628, K629) appear to be involved in binding the negatively-charged DNA backbone.
source: Importantly, there are several positively-charged and aromatic residues in the loops (K591, N595, H596 W626, H628, K629) that appear to be involved in binding the negatively-charged DNA backbone (Figure 4b).
evidence: The manuscript lists specific residues that appear to interact with DNA.

claim: The ORC4 region in HsORC is 20 residues shorter than the ScORC segment and does not contain an α-helix.
source: This region in HsORC is 20 residues shorter than the ScORC segment and does not contain an α-helix (Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 5; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific length difference and describes the absence of an α-helix.

claim: The missing helix in HsORC4 likely reduces its ability to bind specifically to a DNA sequence.
source: The missing helix in HsORC likely reduces its ability to bind specifically to a DNA sequence resulting in the requirement of other mechanisms to establish stable origin interactions.
evidence: The manuscript infers that the missing helix affects DNA binding specificity.

claim: In ScORC, the Orc4 WHD contains an α-helix insertion in the β-hairpin wing (residues 481–489) that inserts into the major groove of ARS-sequence DNA.
source: In S. cerevisiae, this domain contains an α-helix insertion in the β-hairpin wing (residues 481–489) that inserts into the major groove of the ARS-sequence DNA and is a key contributor to conferring sequence specificity for origin recognition (Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the α-helix insertion in ScORC4 and its role in DNA binding.

claim: The ORC4 helix insertion has likely evolved in a small clade of Saccharomyces-related budding yeast species in tandem with a loss of RNAi-mediated transcriptional gene silencing.
source: Based on sequence alignments (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), the ORC4 helix insertion has likely evolved in a small clade of Saccharomyces-related budding yeast species in tandem with a loss of RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated transcriptional gene silencing, while the region is absent in most other eukaryotic organisms, including fungi, plants, and animals, which use RNAi for silencing (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the evolutionary context of the ORC4 helix insertion with citation.

claim: HsORC does not display DNA sequence specific DNA binding.
source: Since HsORC does not display DNA sequence specific DNA binding (Vashee et al., 2003; Vashee et al., 2001), the significant difference in ORC4 between budding yeast and human ORC contributes to the sequence-dependent and -independent origin binding in these species (Figure 4f).
evidence: The manuscript states that HsORC lacks sequence-specific DNA binding with citations.

claim: HsORC binds to specific locations in chromosomes and is most likely targeted to these sites by binding to specific histones and their modifications.
source: HsORC binds to specific locations in chromosomes (Miotto et al., 2016) and unlike ScORC, it is most likely targeted to these sites by binding to specific histones and their modifications (Hossain and Stillman, 2016; Kuo et al., 2012; Long et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes how HsORC is targeted to chromosomal locations with citations.

claim: The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) is necessary for orchestrating the initiation process by binding to origin DNA, recruiting CDC6, and assembling the MCM replicative helicase on DNA.
source: The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) is necessary for orchestrating the initiation process by binding to origin DNA, recruiting CDC6, and assembling the MCM replicative helicase on DNA.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the role of ORC in replication initiation.

claim: The absence of ORC1 revealed a compact, stable complex of ORC2-5.
source: The absence of ORC1 revealed a compact, stable complex of ORC2-5.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding in the abstract.

claim: Introduction of ORC1 opens the complex into several dynamic conformations.
source: Introduction of ORC1 opens the complex into several dynamic conformations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding in the abstract.

claim: Two structures revealed dynamic movements of the ORC1 AAA+ and ORC2 winged-helix domains that likely impact DNA incorporation into the ORC core.
source: Two structures revealed dynamic movements of the ORC1 AAA+ and ORC2 winged-helix domains that likely impact DNA incorporation into the ORC core.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding in the abstract.

claim: A hinge at the ORC5·ORC3 interface may facilitate ORC binding to DNA.
source: Additional twist and pinch motions were observed in an open ORC conformation revealing a hinge at the ORC5·ORC3 interface that may facilitate ORC binding to DNA.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding in the abstract.

claim: A structure of ORC with endogenous DNA bound in the core reveals important differences between human and yeast origin recognition.
source: Finally, a structure of ORC was determined with endogenous DNA bound in the core revealing important differences between human and yeast origin recognition.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding in the abstract.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, ORC specifically recognizes and binds to autonomously replicating sequences (ARSs).
source: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, ORC specifically recognizes and binds to a class of DNA sequences, called the autonomously replicating sequences (ARSs), which act as the replication initiation sites in vivo (Bell and Stillman, 1992; Brewer and Fangman, 1987; Eaton et al., 2010; Huberman, 1987; Linskens and Huberman, 1988; Marahrens and Stillman, 1992; Rao and Stillman, 1995; Theis et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript states this with multiple citations.

claim: In metazoans, the manner in which origins are identified is not yet clear.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, this is a sequence-specific binding event, however, in metazoans the manner in which origins are identified is not yet clear.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the uncertainty about origin identification in metazoans.

claim: The BAH-domain at the N-terminus of ORC1 facilitates binding of ORC to DNA through nucleosomes which contain specific histone modifications.
source: The bromo-adjacent homology (BAH)-domain at the N-terminus of ORC1 facilitates binding of ORC to DNA through nucleosomes which contain specific histone modifications that influence ORC1 affinity to the chromatin complex (Eaton et al., 2010; Hossain and Stillman, 2016; Kuo et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2010; Noguchi et al., 2006; Rivera et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the role of the BAH domain with multiple citations.

claim: Single molecule studies have shown that ORC is released from DNA immediately following stable association of two MCM molecules with the DNA substrate.
source: In fact, single molecule studies have shown that ORC is released from DNA immediately following stable association of two MCM molecules with the DNA substrate (Ticau et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a single molecule study showing ORC release.

claim: High resolution structures of ORC from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Drosophila melanogaster, and Homo sapiens have revealed the detailed architecture of the complex.
source: High resolution structures of ORC from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ScORC), Drosophila melanogaster (DmORC), and Homo sapiens (HsORC) have revealed the detailed architecture of the complex (Bleichert et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Tocilj et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple structural studies of ORC from different species.

claim: The ORC complex consists of six subunits (ORC1-6), with subunits ORC1-5 forming a partial ring capable of encircling DNA.
source: The complex consists of six subunits (ORC1-6), with subunits ORC1-5 forming a partial ring capable of encircling DNA (Li et al., 2018; Tocilj et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ORC architecture with citations.

claim: All five ORC subunits contain a winged-helix domain (WHD) and a AAA+ domain which consists of the RecA-fold and lid domains.
source: All five subunits contain a winged-helix domain (WHD) and a AAA+ domain which consists of the RecA-fold and lid domains (Figure 1a), although the ORC2 and ORC3 RecA-folds have diverged slightly and do not contain a lid domain.
evidence: The manuscript describes the domain architecture of ORC subunits.

claim: ORC exhibits two main conformations: an open state and a closed, auto-inhibited state.
source: Based on the previous structures, ORC exhibits two main conformations differing primarily in the positions of the ORC1 AAA+- and ORC2 WH-domains: an open state (ScORC and HsORC) (Li et al., 2018; Tocilj et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2017) and a closed, auto-inhibited state (DmORC) (Bleichert et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes two main ORC conformations with citations.

claim: In the open state, the ORC1 AAA+-domain binds to the ORC4 AAA+-fold to form the ORC1·4 ATPase active site.
source: In the open state, the ORC1 AAA+-domain binds to the ORC4 AAA+-fold to form the ORC1·4 ATPase active site and ORC2 WHD is adjacent to the ORC3 WHD.
evidence: The manuscript describes the open state conformation.

claim: In the closed state, the ORC1 AAA+ motif is dramatically rotated by ~80° towards the ORC2 WHD position.
source: In the closed state, the ORC1 AAA+ motif is dramatically rotated by ~80° towards the ORC2 WHD position and ORC2 WHD is collapsed into the open ring-shaped core of the complex.
evidence: The manuscript describes the closed state conformation with a specific rotation angle.

claim: The collapsed ORC1 AAA+-domain and ORC2 WHD in the closed state completely obstruct the core of ORC and could not accommodate DNA.
source: The collapsed ORC1 AAA+-domain and ORC2 WHD in the closed state completely obstruct the core of ORC and could not accommodate DNA.
evidence: The manuscript describes the consequence of the closed state.

claim: Recent cryoEM studies on HsORC suggested that the ORC1 AAA+ domain also adopts the auto-inhibited conformation.
source: Initially, the closed state was only seen in DmORC, but recent cryoEM studies on HsORC suggested that the ORC1 AAA+ domain also adopts the auto-inhibited conformation (Bleichert et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study showing the auto-inhibited state in HsORC.

claim: In ScORC, the Orc2 ISM binds to the DNA minor groove with the W396 sidechain tucked into the hydrophobic minor groove at the T-rich region.
source: The Orc2 ISM binds to the DNA minor groove with the W396 sidechain tucked into the hydrophobic minor groove at the T-rich region within the ARS consensus DNA sequence (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the Orc2 ISM interaction with DNA in ScORC with citation.

claim: In metazoans, ORC lacks sequence specificity for origin recognition and may rely on interactions with nucleosomes.
source: In metazoans, notably, ORC lacks sequence specificity for origin recognition and may rely on interactions with nucleosomes to establish DNA origin sites (Noguchi et al., 2006; Remus et al., 2004; Vashee et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript states that metazoan ORC lacks sequence specificity with citations.

claim: The ORC1 AAA+ domain in human ORC appears to be dynamic along a continuum of positions between the auto-inhibited state and when it forms the ORC1·4 interface with ORC4.
source: While ORC1 AAA+ is locked in the auto-inhibited state in DmORC, the ORC1 AAA+ domain in human ORC appears to be dynamic along a continuum of positions between two extreme states: the auto-inhibited state observed in the DmORC and when it forms the ORC1·4 interface with ORC4 as observed in ORCO1AAA.
evidence: The manuscript describes the dynamic nature of ORC1 AAA+ in human ORC.

claim: The ORC1 AAA+ domain's dynamic movements may be a consequence of ORC1·4 ATP hydrolysis.
source: The ORC1 AAA+ domain's dynamic movements may be a consequence of ORC1·4 ATP hydrolysis, but further investigation is necessary.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the cause of ORC1 AAA+ dynamics.

claim: ATP promotes the assembly and stability of the human ORC.
source: Based on this idea and previous studies using mutant ORC4 and ORC5 subunits (Siddiqui and Stillman, 2007), we conclude that ATP promotes the assembly and stability of the human ORC, which, unlike yeast ORC, is assembled and disassembled throughout the cell division cycle.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that ATP promotes ORC assembly based on data and citations.

claim: A minor ORC2 WHD conformation was observed in further 3D classifications of the ORCO2WH particles that resembles the completely collapsed ORC2 WHD conformations in the ORCO2-5 structure.
source: A minor ORC2 WHD conformation was observed in further 3D classifications of the ORCO2WH particles (Figure 2e). Secondary structure elements can be seen in the ORC2 WHD region that are clearly different from the auto-inhibited conformation. In fact, this conformation resembles the completely collapsed ORC2 WHD conformations in the ORCO2-5 structure where the domain is further tucked into the core of the complex compared to the auto-inhibited state (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript describes an alternative ORC2 WHD conformation observed in 3D classification.

claim: The buried ORC2 WHD appears to stabilize ORC2-5 complex prior to ORC1 binding, hence termed the inactive state.
source: The buried ORC2 WHD appears to stabilize ORC2-5 complex prior to ORC1 binding, hence we termed this structure of the ORC2 WHD the inactive state (Figure 1b and Figure 2c,e).
evidence: The manuscript infers the function of the buried ORC2 WHD and names it the inactive state.

claim: The binding of ORC1 seems to facilitate the release of the O2 WHD from the tucked-in state.
source: The binding of ORC1 seems to facilitate the release of the O2 WHD from this tucked-in state, generating a more labile structure for downstream events.
evidence: The manuscript infers that ORC1 binding releases ORC2 WHD from the inactive state.

claim: In both the yeast OCCM and ORC-DNA structures, the ORC2 WHD interacts with the origin DNA.
source: In both the yeast OCCM and ORC-DNA structures (Li et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2017), the ORC2 WHD interacts with the origin DNA and is far away from the gap between the ORC1 and ORC2 AAA+ domains, forming a collar of ORC WHDs that surround the DNA.
evidence: The manuscript cites yeast structures showing ORC2 WHD-DNA interactions.

claim: The movement of the ORC2 WHD seems to be a universal feature of controlling DNA access to the ring-shaped core of ORC.
source: Thus the movement of the ORC2 WHD seems to be a universal feature of controlling DNA access to the ring-shaped core of ORC and hence binding to DNA.
evidence: The manuscript infers that ORC2 WHD movement is a universal feature based on observations.

claim: The long helix in ORCOPEN may provide structural stability to the open conformation.
source: This long helix in ORCOPEN may provide structural stability to the open conformation.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the function of the long helix in ORCOPEN.

claim: Both Multibody Refinement and 3D Variability Analysis revealed the same prominent movements in the ORCO1AAA particle population.
source: Both Multibody Refinement and 3D Variability Analysis revealed the same prominent movements in the ORCO1AAA particle population.
evidence: The manuscript states that two different methods yielded the same results.

claim: The ORC twisting motion involves ORC1 and ORC2 sliding over each other.
source: The ORC twisting motion involves ORC1 and ORC2 sliding over each other, while the pinching motion involves ORC1 and ORC2 narrowing/widening the ORC ring opening between them (Figure 3c,d and Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the twisting motion.

claim: The pinching motion involves ORC1 and ORC2 narrowing/widening the ORC ring opening between them.
source: The ORC twisting motion involves ORC1 and ORC2 sliding over each other, while the pinching motion involves ORC1 and ORC2 narrowing/widening the ORC ring opening between them (Figure 3c,d and Video 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the pinching motion.

claim: The twisting and pinching movements provide potential flexibility to ORC during replication initiation events.
source: The twisting and pinching movements provide potential flexibility to ORC during replication initiation events, including DNA binding, movement along DNA, and/or complex release after MCM double hexamer formation.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the functional significance of the observed movements.

claim: The DNA fragment visualized in ORCDNA is likely a result of a superposition of sequences along the DNA fragment.
source: Since DNA-binding of HsORC is not sequence specific, the DNA is likely to have multiple orientations along its axis in the core, consistent with further 3D classification of the DNA-bound ORC populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). In other words, the DNA fragment visualized is a result of a superposition of sequences along the DNA fragment.
evidence: The manuscript infers that the DNA density represents a superposition due to lack of sequence specificity.

claim: The overall conformation of ORCDNA resembles the more closed conformations of ORCO1AAA and ORCO2WH.
source: The overall conformation of ORCDNA resembles the more closed conformations of ORCO1AAA and ORCO2WH, albeit with ORC2 WHD in a different conformation (see below).
evidence: The manuscript compares the ORCDNA conformation to other structures.

claim: Most of the ORC1 DNA-binding residues are conserved in vertebrate species but differ in insects, plants and fungi.
source: Sequence alignments show that while most of these residues are conserved in vertebrate species, they differ in insects, plants and fungi (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes sequence conservation patterns based on alignments.

claim: The ORC2 WHD may adopt multiple conformations in ORCDNA similar to the multiple ORC2 WHD states observed in DNA-bound ScORC.
source: The ORC2 WHD may adopt multiple conformations in this structure similar to the multiple ORC2 WHD states observed in DNA-bound ScORC (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about ORC2 WHD conformations based on comparison to ScORC.

claim: The positively-charged ORC2 residue R367 appears to mediate the interaction with DNA.
source: Specifically, the positively-charged ORC2 residue R367 emanating from this loop, appears to mediate the interaction with DNA.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a specific residue that appears to interact with DNA.

claim: The ORC2 ISM in humans may play an important role in binding DNA similar to the ORC2 ISM in ScORC.
source: The ORC2 ISM in humans may play an important role in binding DNA similar to the ORC2 ISM in ScORC where W396 is buried in the minor groove of DNA (Li et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the role of ORC2 ISM in humans based on comparison to yeast.

claim: The β-hairpin loop in ORC5 of HsORC consists of a positively-charged residue H398 in close proximity to DNA.
source: The β-hairpin loop in ORC5 of HsORC also consists of a positively-charged residue H398 in close proximity to DNA (Figure 4a,f).
evidence: The manuscript identifies a specific residue in ORC5 near DNA.

claim: The β-hairpin loop in ORC5 of ScORC contains positively-charged residues extending into the major groove of DNA.
source: Similarly, the β-hairpin loop in ORC5 of ScORC contains positively-charged residues (N438, K439, N440, K447, R449) extending into the major groove of DNA (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites the ScORC structure showing ORC5 residues interacting with DNA.

claim: The Orc4 WHD plays an important role in origin-specific binding in S. cerevisiae.
source: The Orc4 WHD plays an important role in origin-specific binding in S. cerevisiae (Hu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing the importance of Orc4 WHD in yeast.

claim: The homologous ORC4 region in HsORC is visible in the ORCO1AAA cryoEM density map.
source: The homologous ORC4 region in HsORC is visible in the ORCO1AAA cryoEM density map allowing us to now model this region (Figure 4e).
evidence: The manuscript states that the ORC4 region was modeled in the ORCO1AAA structure.

claim: The loss of the helix in HsORC4 contributes to the multiple conformations of DNA observed in the core of human ORC.
source: This loss of specificity also contributes to the multiple conformations of DNA observed in the core of human ORC (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript infers that the missing helix contributes to DNA conformational heterogeneity.

claim: The shorter ORC4 loop contacts the DNA in the ORCDNA structure proximal to R390.
source: Despite the missing helix, the shorter ORC4 loop contacts the DNA in the ORCDNA structure proximal to R390 (Figure 4e), a positively-charged residue that may participate in DNA-backbone interactions similar to R478 in ScORC4 (Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript describes DNA contact by the ORC4 loop in ORCDNA.

claim: The significant difference in ORC4 between budding yeast and human ORC contributes to the sequence-dependent and -independent origin binding in these species.
source: Since HsORC does not display DNA sequence specific DNA binding (Vashee et al., 2003; Vashee et al., 2001), the significant difference in ORC4 between budding yeast and human ORC contributes to the sequence-dependent and -independent origin binding in these species (Figure 4f).
evidence: The manuscript infers that ORC4 differences contribute to DNA binding specificity differences.

claim: ORC1 may recruit the other subunits via interactions facilitated by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in the N-terminal regions of ORC1 and ORC2.
source: Since ORC1 appears to be the first ORC subunit to bind to chromosomes during mitosis (Kara et al., 2015; Okuno et al., 2001), ORC1 may recruit the other subunits via the pathway outlined in Figure 5.
